questions.question: Matter is any substance that
questions.explanation: Matter is defined by two essential properties: it has mass (it can be weighed) and it occupies space (it has volume). Option B is wrong because shape is not universal — liquids and gases have no fixed shape. Option C confuses matter with energy (light and heat have energy but are not matter). Option D describes specific properties that only some matter has — gases have very low density, and many substances do not dissolve.

questions.question: Plasma is best described as
options: Gas cooled to liquid or solid
Liquids and gases with weak forces
questions.explanation: Plasma is the fourth state of matter — a superheated gas in which electrons have been stripped from atoms, producing a mixture of free electrons and positive ions. It is the most abundant state in the universe (stars, lightning, neon signs). Option A describes condensation, not plasma. Option B describes a solid. Option D describes the weak intermolecular forces in fluids, not plasma.

questions.question: Which state has definite volume but no definite shape?
questions.explanation: Liquids have a definite volume (they cannot easily be compressed) but no definite shape (they take the shape of their container). Option A (solid) has both definite shape and definite volume. Option C (gas) has neither. Option D (plasma) has neither.

questions.question: Which is a physical property?
questions.explanation: A physical property can be observed without changing the substance's chemical identity. Melting point is physical — ice melts to water and remains H2O. Options A, B, and C describe chemical properties: flammability (reacts with oxygen), toxicity (interferes with biological chemistry), and acidity (ability to donate H+) all describe how a substance reacts chemically.

questions.question: Which is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: A chemical change produces a new substance with different chemical properties. Burning paper turns cellulose into CO2, H2O, and ash — new substances. Options A (melting), B (cutting), and D (dissolving) are physical changes: the substance changes state or shape but retains its chemical identity.

questions.question: A pure substance is made up of
questions.explanation: A pure substance contains only one kind of particle — either atoms of a single element (e.g. copper) or molecules of a single compound (e.g. H2O). It has a fixed, sharp melting and boiling point. Option A describes a mixture. Option B describes variable composition — pure substances have fixed composition. Option D is contradictory — a mixture is by definition not pure.

questions.question: Which is a homogeneous mixture?
questions.explanation: A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition throughout — you cannot see the separate components. Sugar dissolved in water is uniform. Option A (sand + water) is heterogeneous — sand settles. Option B (oil + water) is heterogeneous — oil floats in a separate layer. Option C is wrong because dust suspended in air is heterogeneous — you can see the particles.

questions.question: Smallest particle of an element that can enter chemical combination?
questions.explanation: The atom is the smallest particle of an element that can enter into chemical combination while retaining the element's identity. Option A (molecule) is a group of atoms, larger than a single atom. Option B (ion) is a charged particle — atoms can enter combination without being charged. Option D (radical) is a group of atoms acting as a unit.

questions.question: Atomicity of oxygen as O<sub>2</sub>?
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule. Oxygen gas is O2 — two oxygen atoms bonded together, so it is diatomic. Option A (monoatomic) describes noble gases like He and Ne. Option C (triatomic) describes O3 (ozone). Option D (polyatomic) describes molecules with many atoms, like P4 or S8.

questions.question: Cations are formed by
questions.explanation: A cation is a positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons (e.g. Na → Na+ + e−). Option A (gain of electrons) produces an anion (negatively charged). Option C (sharing) is covalent bonding, not ion formation. Option D is impossible — protons are locked inside the nucleus.

questions.question: Which is a radical?
questions.explanation: A radical (or polyatomic ion) is a group of atoms that behaves as a single unit in chemical reactions and carries a charge. CN− (cyanide) is a classic example. Option A (Cl) is a single atom. Option B (O2) is a neutral molecule. Option D (Na) is a single metal atom.

questions.question: Chemical symbol for sodium based on Latin name?
questions.explanation: The symbol for sodium is Na, from its Latin name natrium. This is why Na does not obviously match sodium in English. Options A, B, and C are not real element symbols. Other Latin-derived symbols to remember: K (potassium, kalium), Fe (iron, ferrum), Cu (copper, cuprum), Pb (lead, plumbum), Au (gold, aurum).

questions.question: In formula Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, number of oxygen atoms?
questions.explanation: In Al2(SO4)3, the subscript 3 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside: SO4 × 3 = S3O12. So there are 12 oxygen atoms. Option A (4) counts only one SO4 group. Option C (3) counts the number of sulfur atoms or the bracket multiplier. Option B (7) is incorrect arithmetic.

questions.question: When writing formula of metal and nonmetal, which symbol is written first?
questions.explanation: The convention is that the metal is written first, then the nonmetal. Examples: NaCl (not ClNa), MgO (not OMg), CaCO3. Option A reverses the convention. Option C ignores the rule. Option D is not applicable — radicals follow the same rule.

questions.question: Which of these shows the combining of an atom?
questions.explanation: Valency is the combining power (or capacity) of an atom — the number of electrons it can gain, lose, or share to form bonds. Sodium has valency 1; oxygen has valency 2. Note: the source marked Molar Mass as the answer, but this is incorrect — molar mass (the mass of one mole of a substance) has nothing to do with combining capacity. Pressure, temperature, and molar mass are unrelated to how atoms bond.

questions.question: Formula for calcium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Calcium (Ca) has valency 2 and hydroxide (OH) has valency 1. Cross-multiplying gives Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>. Option A has the wrong ratio (1:1). Option B has incorrect subscript on calcium. Option D is a made-up formula — CaH<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is not calcium hydroxide.

questions.question: Relative atomic mass is compared to
questions.explanation: Relative atomic mass (RAM) is defined as the average mass of an atom compared to 1/12 the mass of one carbon-12 atom. This is the modern IUPAC standard. Option A was used historically but is obsolete. Option C was used in older textbooks but was replaced. Option D (mass of a proton) is not the standard — protons, neutrons, and electrons contribute differently to the mass.

questions.question: Relative molecular mass of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>?
questions.explanation: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1. Ca(OH)2 = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 2 × 17 = 74. Option B (40) is just the calcium contribution. Option A (57) and D (58) are miscalculations. Always expand the bracket: the subscript 2 applies to both O and H.

questions.question: Avogadro's number is
questions.explanation: Avogadro's number is approximately 6.022 × 1023 — the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in one mole of a substance. Option B has a negative exponent — that's a tiny number, not Avogadro's. Option C is a made-up value. Option D (1.602 × 1019) is the charge on an electron in coulombs — an entirely different constant.

questions.question: Molar mass unit is
questions.explanation: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in g/mol. Example: water has molar mass 18 g/mol. Option A (g) is mass, not molar mass. Option B (mol) is the amount of substance. Option C (amu) is used for individual atoms — relative atomic mass has no unit because it is a ratio.

questions.question: Mass of 2 moles H<sub>2</sub>O (H=1, O=16)?
questions.explanation: Molar mass of H2O = 2(1) + 16 = 18 g/mol. Mass = moles × molar mass = 2 × 18 = 36 g. Option A (18 g) is the mass of just one mole. Option B (20 g) is a miscalculation. Option D (44 g) is the molar mass of CO2, not water.

questions.question: Number of moles in 500 g CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O (Mm=249.5)?
questions.explanation: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 500 ÷ 249.5 = 2.004 ≈ 2.00 mol. Option A would require 249.5 g. Option C would require 124.75 g. Option B would require 623.75 g. Always divide the given mass by the molar mass.

questions.question: Percentage of oxygen in CaCO<sub>3</sub> (Ca=40, C=12, O=16)?
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100 g/mol. Mass of oxygen = 3 × 16 = 48 g. Percentage = (48 ÷ 100) × 100 = 48%. Option A (16%) is a single O atom. Option B (40%) is the calcium contribution. Option C (12%) is the carbon contribution.

questions.question: Empirical formula shows
questions.explanation: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. Example: hydrogen peroxide's molecular formula is H2O2, but its empirical formula is HO. Option A describes the molecular formula. Option B is a mass, not a formula. Option D is unrelated.

questions.question: If empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O and molar mass 180, molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Mass of empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O = 12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30. Divide molar mass by empirical mass: 180 ÷ 30 = 6. Multiply all subscripts by 6: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> (glucose). Option A is the empirical formula itself. Options B and C are intermediate multiples (×3 and ×2).

questions.question: Law of conservation of matter states
options: Matter can be created from energy
Matter can neither be created nor destroyed
Matter changes mass with changing volume
Matter is indestructible only in solids
questions.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. Option A is incorrect for ordinary chemical reactions (nuclear reactions can convert mass to energy, but that is not chemistry). Option C is unrelated. Option D is false — the law applies to all states.

questions.question: Law of definite proportion proposed by
questions.explanation: The Law of Definite Proportions was proposed by Joseph Proust: a chemical compound always contains its component elements in a fixed ratio by mass. Water is always 8:1 hydrogen to oxygen by mass, whether from a tap or a well. Option A (Dalton) proposed atomic theory. Option B (Gay-Lussac) worked on gas volumes. Option C (Avogadro) gave the mole concept.

questions.question: CO and CO<sub>2</sub> illustrate
questions.explanation: The Law of Multiple Proportions states that when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios. In CO and CO2, the oxygen masses combining with 12 g of carbon are 16 g and 32 g — ratio 1:2. Option A is about mass conservation. Options B and D are different laws.

questions.question: Law of reciprocal proportions involves
options: Masses combining with fixed mass of another element
Volumes of gases combining at constant temperature and pressure
Partial pressures of different gases combining
questions.explanation: The Law of Reciprocal Proportions states that if two elements A and B combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element C, then the ratio in which A and B combine with each other is a simple whole-number ratio of the ratios in which they combined with C. Option B describes Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes. Option C is Dalton's law of partial pressures. Option D is the combined gas law.

questions.question: In chemical equation, arrow means
questions.explanation: The arrow → in a chemical equation means produces or yields — it separates reactants (left) from products (right). Option A is wrong — the arrow does not mean equal to. Option B is wrong — a reversible reaction uses ⇌ (double arrow). Option D is wrong — heat is indicated by Δ above the arrow.

questions.question: Which symbol shows that the substance is dissolved in water?
questions.explanation: (aq) stands for aqueous — the substance is dissolved in water. Option A (g) means gas. Option B (s) means solid. Option C (l) means pure liquid (not dissolved in water). The distinction matters — NaCl(s) is table salt, NaCl(aq) is salt water.

questions.question: Balanced equation has equal
questions.explanation: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides — this is required by the Law of Conservation of Mass. Option A is incorrect — the number of moles of reactants and products is not necessarily equal. Option C is incorrect — molecules rearrange. Option D is incorrect — gas volumes are governed by Avogadro's law, not by balancing.

questions.question: Balance: H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> → HI. Correct coefficients?
questions.explanation: H2 + I2 → 2HI. Left side: 2 H, 2 I. Right side: 2 H, 2 I. Balanced as 1,1,2. Option A has only 1 H and 1 I on the right — unbalanced. Option B is a multiple of the simplest ratio (2:1:2 vs 1:1:2) — chemically valid but not the simplest form. Convention prefers the simplest whole-number coefficients.

questions.question: In 2Na + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaOH + H<sub>2</sub>, 2 moles H<sub>2</sub>O produce how many moles H<sub>2</sub>?
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows 2 moles H2O → 1 mole H2. The mole ratio H2O:H2 is 2:1. So 2 moles of water give 1 mole of hydrogen gas. Options A, B, and C ignore the stoichiometric ratio — always read the coefficients.

questions.question: Stoichiometry is based on
questions.explanation: Stoichiometry is the calculation of quantities of reactants and products in a chemical reaction, based on the balanced equation. The coefficients give the mole ratios. Options A, B, and D are physical properties unrelated to reaction quantities.

questions.question: Combination reaction general equation
questions.explanation: A combination reaction joins two or more substances into one product: A + X → AX. Option A is decomposition (one → many). Option C is single-replacement. Option D is double-replacement.

questions.question: Decomposition of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> gives
questions.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide decomposes on heating: Mg(OH)2 → MgO + H2O. The elements do not separate into their raw atomic forms — the hydroxide group breaks down into oxide and water. Options A, B, and C all produce elemental forms, which is not what happens for this hydroxide decomposition.

questions.question: Combustion reactions are usually
questions.explanation: Combustion (burning) releases heat and light — it is exothermic. Every combustion reaction has a negative enthalpy change. Option A is wrong — endothermic reactions absorb heat (e.g. photosynthesis). Option B is not applicable. Option D is wrong — combustion is essentially irreversible under normal conditions.

questions.question: Cu + 2AgNO<sub>3</sub> → Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2Ag is
questions.explanation: In this reaction, copper replaces silver in silver nitrate. One element (Cu) displaces another (Ag) from its compound — that is a single-replacement reaction. Option A joins substances. Option B breaks substances apart. Option C exchanges partners between two compounds (which would involve two compounds swapping ions).

questions.question: Double-replacement reaction often produces
questions.explanation: In a double-replacement reaction, two compounds exchange partners. If one of the products is insoluble in water, it forms a solid precipitate. Example: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO3(aq) — AgCl is the precipitate. Option B is possible but not the most common outcome. Option C applies to exothermic reactions generally. Option D would indicate a single-replacement reaction.

questions.question: NaCl(aq) + AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) is
questions.explanation: Na+ and Ag+ swap anions — Na pairs with NO3− and Ag pairs with Cl−. Two compounds exchange partners, making this a double-replacement reaction. The AgCl(s) precipitate confirms it. Option A would be one element displacing another. Options B and C are wrong by definition.

questions.question: Kinetic theory states particles of matter are
questions.explanation: The Kinetic Theory of Matter states that all particles of matter are in constant random motion. The higher the temperature, the faster the motion. Option A is the opposite of the theory. Option B confuses atoms with the theory — particles have kinetic energy. Option D is wrong because most particles are not charged.

questions.question: Diffusion is fastest in
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the movement of particles from high to low concentration. It is fastest in gases because gas particles have the most energy and the largest interparticle spaces, so they move freely. Option A (solids) is slowest — particles are locked in place. Option B (liquids) is intermediate. Option C (plasma) is not typically compared in this context.

questions.question: Brownian motion is caused by
questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the random jiggling of tiny suspended particles due to collisions with invisible molecules of the surrounding fluid. Option A is wrong because the molecules hitting the particles are too small to see individually. Options C and D are not involved — Brownian motion is a collision phenomenon, not a force phenomenon.

questions.question: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, volume is
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law states that at constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant, so volume and pressure are inversely proportional — as pressure rises, volume falls. Option A would be Charles's law for temperature. Option B is not a law. Option C is false — volume and pressure are related.

questions.question: Charles's law relates volume to
questions.explanation: Charles's Law states that at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute (Kelvin) temperature: V/T = constant. Options A and B refer to pressure, which is the variable held constant in Charles's law. Option D is unrelated.

questions.question: Gay-Lussac's law states pressure is directly proportional to
questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac's Law (also called the pressure-temperature law) states that at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature: P/T = constant. Options A, B, and C are unrelated quantities.

questions.question: Ideal gas law equation
questions.explanation: The Ideal Gas Law combines all the individual gas laws into one equation: PV = nRT, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = gas constant, T = temperature. Option A is Boyle's law. Option B is Charles's law. Option D is Gay-Lussac's law.

questions.question: Dalton's law of partial pressures: total pressure equals
questions.explanation: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each gas: Ptotal = P1 + P2 + P3 + ... Option A would produce a meaningless product. Option B mixes the concept with averages. Option C subtracts, which is wrong.

questions.question: Graham's law of diffusion: rate is inversely proportional to
questions.explanation: Graham's Law states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass: Rate ∝ 1/√M. Lighter gases diffuse faster — this is why helium escapes from balloons much faster than CO2. Option A omits the square root. Options B and C are unrelated to Graham's law.
